history.note: Jacobs 1864 (published eyewitness, Gettysburg resident), under the printed heading "Thursday, June 25.": "Late on Thursday evening, however, 100 picked ... But the heavy rain of that night caused them to be detained" (p.14). Under the heading "Friday, June 26.": "Being wet from the rain which had fallen during the most of the day" (p.16). Supports: heavy rain the night of 25 Jun and rain most of 26 Jun. Sub-claim tier: documented (single published eyewitness, no clock time). It gives no start hour for the 25 Jun rain, so it neither confirms the PDF "8 am" nor the 1885 "8 p.m."; the proposal word "contradicted" is NOT adopted (rain earlier on the 25th is not excluded by "that night"). Fremantle (British observer with the Confederate army), diary of 4 Jul: "At 1 p. M. the rain began to descend in toiTents" (p.274, OCR) and "Shortly after 9 p. m. the rain began to descend in torrents." (p.276); the following entry has "thunder and lightning, torrents of rain". Sub-claim tier: documented as one witness statement (his clock, Confederate side, place not stated). Added as a selectable Jul 4 rain scenario (13:00 and after 21:00). Existing schedules are not deleted and not refuted. Comparison with the named preset schedules was not re-checked in this review. Letterman 1866 p.156: "drenching rain which fell after the battle" (no hour). NOT touched: humidity, pressure, 87 F in shade, Jul 2 14:00 cloud, Jul 3 rainfall, Union-side Jul 4 clock. Entry remains open.

title: Road of approach modelled from the sibling formations of the corps (history layer v6)
desc: No report of the Official Records read for the position ledgers (OR vol. 27) prints a road of approach for 56 leaf units (Longstreet's corps except Kershaw, Semmes, Wofford and Pickett's brigades; the Fifth Corps except the 20th Maine and Day's division) or for any formation above them. Each is drawn by the road that every documented sibling formation of its corps names (Chambersburg Pike for the First Corps, from Kershaw's report; Hanover Road for the Fifth Corps, from the 20th Maine row and Day's division report). The sibling formations may not have been on the road the unit used.
why: The record read so far does not state the unit's road; the primary sources are unread in part (EG-0005) and the Official Records give only some brigades' routes. Literal documentation of the road of these 56 units is not available from the repository.
searched: The four OR27 position ledgers (history/positions/positions_{A,B,C,D}.jsonl, 3,503 claims), every claim that names a road on the lines of command (APPROACH-AUDIT.md, data/sibling-review.json), the road-name concordance (library/ROAD-CONCORDANCE.md). Not yet searched: the regimental and brigade reports not in the ledgers, Busey and Martin, state regimental histories.
subst: Sibling-road rule (DEC-015): the units take the road documented for the other formations of their corps only if every documented sibling names the same road and no report on the unit's line of command names another road, a road the repository cannot place or a road outside the loaded ground (tools/sibling-rule.mjs, data/sibling-approach.json).
recon: A MODELLED road of approach (plausible-procedural). The unit's gate (never moved), its single-label Bachelder day position and its march from the edge of the ground are as for any other drawn unit; only the road, the minute at the edge and the place in the column are modelled.
marking: Card pill 'Modelled approach'; card text 'MODELLED APPROACH' with the siblings listed (report, page, printed words); provenance row 'Approach road (modelled)'; link to this entry; about panel paragraph.
impact: 56 leaf units (about 17,300 figures) in the First and Fifth Corps.
owner_q: Accept the sibling-road rule (DEC-015), reverse it (delete data/sibling-approach.json and the units return to open gaps) or require two or more documented siblings.
rec: Keep it as marked until the reports of the brigades are read; do not read it as history.

title: Faces, hair, facial hair, skin tone and body shape of every enlisted man (figure models)
desc: No record gives any enlisted man's face, hair, beard, complexion, stature or build (see EG-0001). The figure models generate every man from his manifest seed: 24 head shapes, 8 hair styles, 7 facial-hair types, 12 skin tones, 5 eye colours, 12 body shapes, stature 0.95-1.06 of 1.73 m. The mixes (facial hair 30/22/6/18/6/6/12 percent, hair colours, skin-tone weights, grey share 12 percent, coat-off share on 1-3 July) are tuning weights.
why: Literal 100% is impossible: individual appearance of the 165,000 men was not recorded. No anthropometric table, photograph survey or muster-roll physical description set was read for this task.
searched: kit/kit_specs.json (wear_states, no appearance data), PDF Part B.6 (dress only), render/PLAN.md G8 (variation targets). Not searched: enlistment descriptive rolls (height, complexion, hair, eyes are printed on Union enlistment papers: a possible source for sampled distributions), Gould 1869 anthropometry, CDV surveys.
subst: Seeded deterministic generation: the same man always has the same face; distributions are tuning parameters recorded in data/figures3d/TIERS.json (F-FACE, F-DIST-*, F-GAP-COMPLEXION).
recon: Generic adult male proportions with varied faces; no distribution is claimed to match any army or unit.
marking: Tier overlay glyph on every individual (EG-0001 marking); card text names the figure as a generated individual; TIERS.json F-FACE.
owner_q: Provide or allow the descriptive-roll sources (for example the printed height, complexion, hair and eye colour on Union enlistment records) so the distributions can be sampled from data; until then they stay tuning weights.
rec: Keep it marked until the source exists; do not read it as history.

title: Star count and arrangement of the US national colour
desc: The national colour is drawn with 34 stars on 13 stripes. No repository text states a star count for the flags at Gettysburg. The count rests on statutory reasoning recalled from memory (a star is added on the 4 July following an admission; West Virginia was admitted 20 June 1863, so 34 stars were in law on 1-3 July 1863): the lookup was NOT performed in this task. The arrangement (rows 6-5-6-5-6-6) is a plausible choice; period flags varied.
why: The record read so far does not describe any regiment's national colour; individual flags carried other star counts and arrangements.
searched: The repository (kit, PDF B.6, history layer): no star count. Not searched: the Flag Act of 1818 text, regimental colour catalogues (state flag collections), photographs of colours.
subst: A 34-star national colour; tier inferred (statutory reasoning) with the lookup recorded as not done.
recon: Stars and stripes with 34 stars in a plausible arrangement.
marking: Tier overlay on the flag; TIERS.json F-STAR-COUNT / F-STAR-ARRANGEMENT; FIGURES3D-NOTES.md.
impact: Every Union national colour drawn (the manifest gives a flag to a small share of men per unit).
owner_q: Run the lookup (statute text, state flag collections for the regiments' colours) so the count and arrangement can be documented per regiment.
rec: Keep it marked until the source exists; do not read it as history.

title: Union regimental and state colours, Irish Brigade flag device, cavalry guidon, colour-guard structure, flag sizes
desc: The repository holds no description of any Union regimental or state colour (kit item regimental_color_union: "pattern not specified in B.6"), no device of the Irish Brigade green flags (flag_green_irish), no guidon designation (guidon_swallowtail_cav: "unsourced in the notes"), no colour-guard structure and no flag sizes. The figures draw the national colour; the regimental colour is a hatched GAP-colour flag; the Irish flag is plain green with a hatched edge; the guidon is a swallow-tail with stars and stripes, no designation. Who carries a flag follows the manifest's "few" draw (a tuning weight), not a documented colour guard.
why: Regimental colours were individual objects; the repository has no catalogue of them.
searched: kit/kit_specs.json items and units, PDF B.6.2-B.6.15 (flags are generic). Not searched: state flag collections (Pennsylvania Capitol flag collection, New York State Military Museum), regimental histories, the NPS flag records.
subst: Marked placeholders as described; no regimental colour is invented.
recon: National colour (inferred star count) plus visibly marked gap colours.
marking: Hatched GAP colour flag; instance flag bit 7 and variant gap_items count; TIERS.json F-REGIMENTAL-COLOUR, F-IRISH-GREEN, F-GUIDON, F-FLAG-SIZE, F-BEARER-RULE.
owner_q: Authorise the search of state flag collections and regimental histories for the colours of the 87 Union regiments drawn.
rec: Keep it marked until the source exists; do not read it as history.

title: Uniform and material colour values, dye variation, wear and soiling

Every sRGB value in the figure palette is ours (plausible-procedural); equal shares are used where a label allows several colours; fading, dust, powder and rain darkening and dye-lot tint are tuning functions of the manifest wear level (itself a tuning parameter: no source quantifies soiling, kit G20). Not read: Taylor 1875 statement, Law postwar essay, McLaws and Hood postwar writings, Bachelder collection. [History 2026-11-11, ws9 source review: Fremantle 1864 pp.256-259; Alexander 1907 pp.391-395; Law in Battles and Leaders vol. 3 pp.319-323 (archive id battlesleadersof03cent, re-fetched hash-verified). Still unread: Hood and McLaws own postwar writings, Taylor 1875, Bachelder collection.]
subst: Carry the OR bounds, the memoir values and the plan clocks as separate scenarios; do not merge or choose.
recon: Carry the OR bounds, the memoir values and the plan clocks as separate scenarios; do not merge or choose. [History 2026-11-11: Additional witness values carried as separate scenarios; none chosen; no merge; tier unchanged.]

history.note: Fremantle (diary, 2 Jul): up at 3.30 A.M.; "arrived at 5 A. M. at the same commanding position" where "Generals Lee, Hill, Longstreet, and Hood" were "in consultation" (p.257): scenario value 05:00 for Hood and Longstreet with Lee. Tier inferred (one diary witness, clock his own). Fremantle p.257: "At Y A. M. I rode over part of the ground with General Longstreet, and saw him disposing of M'Laws's division". The OCR prints the hour as "Y"; 7 is a reading inferred from the sequence of hours, NOT a printed value. Recorded as "07:00 (OCR-uncertain; page-image check required)" and not to be used as a scenario clock until checked. Alexander 1907 (participant, retrospective) p.391: "About 11 A.M., his orders were issued." Second retrospective witness for 11:00; independence from Longstreet 1896 not shown. Hood attack: Alexander p.394 Hood crossed the Emmitsburg road "about 3 P.M."; p.395 "about 3.45 P.M., 36 guns were in action" and "After this cannonade had continued for perhaps 30 minutes, Hood received the order to advance" (an order about 16:15 is arithmetic from those two statements, not printed). Fremantle p.258-259: "A dead silence reigned till 4.45 p. m." then "Longstreet suddenly commenced a heavy cannonade". Law pp.320, 323: "past 4 o'clock" in position; "near 5 o'clock p. M. when we advanced to the attack"; artillery "warmly engaged for about fifteen minutes". The clocks are mutually inconsistent within about an hour; they support a window, not a point. Law p.319: moved at 3 o'clock on the morning of the 2d, "arrived there shortly before noon" (his brigade only, not Hood himself). Fremantle p.258 "Pickett being still in the rear" on 2 Jul is noted for C-021 only; gate Q04 not moved. The register statement that no OR report gives an hour remains true. Tier stays inferred (nothing promoted), status stays open.

history.note: E-001 (Nov 18), narrowed: Everett p.20 "In the afternoon of the 18th, the President and the distinguished personages accompanying him arrived at Gettysburg, by a special train. In the course of the evening, the President and Secretary of State were serenaded, and the following remarks were made by Mr. Seward" (p.20-21); the Sentinel prints that Seward "was serenaded at his lodgings in the Square" with "a brief speech" (no date printed in the fragment). Sub-claims documented: arrival by special train in the afternoon of the 18th; evening serenade; Seward remarks. NOT supported: 18:00 hour, William McDougall, walk uphill to the Wills house, lodging location. The Sentinel line "President ... serenaded twice during the evening" sits in an undated dispatch column (OCR) and is NOT used. E-008 (Marine Band), applied-narrowed: Everett p.12 "The Presidential party was accompanied by the Marine Band from the Navy Yard at Washington"; programme p.25 lists "Music, by the Marine Band." after the prayer; the Sentinel procession list shows a Marine Band entry. Sub-claim tier documented for presence with the Presidential party and for the programmed music; that it played at the platform at that point is programmed, not reported as performed. E-005 (troops salute), applied-narrowed: only the programme p.24 states the military will form in line "for the purpose of saluting the President" (OCR "saluthig"). A plan, not an account. Sub-claim tier: inferred (planned). No report of the act was found. E-014 (church), applied-narrowed with rewording: Sentinel prints "at 5 o'clock p. M. Col. Anderson ... delivered an able address in the Presbyterian church" with "The President of the United States and suite ... occupied seats in the pulpit", and that John Burns "went to church in the evening" arm in arm with the President and Secretary of State (OCR noisy). Reworded sub-claim: 5 p.m. address by Col. Anderson in the Presbyterian church with the President present (the day is placed as the 19th by the article's order, the fragment itself prints no date). Tier documented (one local newspaper, as printed). A religious service and "leaves by train about 18:00" are NOT supported; the Sentinel prints only "left late in the evening". E-002: no statement found; unchanged gap.

title: Hour and text of Lee's order to concentrate at Cashtown or Gettysburg (T1-060)
desc: Row T1-060 (Jun 30 evening). Verdict corrected. Ewell received that order at Heidlersburg on the night of Jun 30, with a note from Hill saying he was at Cashtown; Early was told the object was to concentrate the corps at or near Cashtown. desc: Row T1-063 (Jun 30 NIGHT). Verdict partially_supported. Corrected claim: Gamble's brigade was in camp at the seminary building on the morning of Jul 1; Doubleday places the ridge on which the line was formed about 400 yards west of the seminary, so the camp lay roughly 400 yards east of that ridge for Gamble's brigade. title: Clock time of the seminary steeple scene (Jerome, Buford, Reynolds); the ladder; the original of Jerome's letter (T1-092, T1-093)
desc: Row T1-092 (Jul 1 ≈09:30-10:20). Verdict corrected. Corrected claim: In a letter of 18 October 1865 to Maj. Gen. Hancock (the original is in the Bachelder Papers; it is printed in a 1989 U.S. Army War College study, which was read, the original was not seen) the signal officer Aaron B. Jerome says that he was sent back to find a prominent position and watch the enemy; that as early as seven A.M. he reported their advance and took his station in the steeple of the "Theological Seminary"; that Buford came up and looked at them through his glass and then formed his small cavalry force; that, looking toward Emmitsburg, he called Buford's attention to an army corps advancing about two miles off and distinguished it as the "first" by its "corps flag"; and that Buford held on, unaided, for half an hour against a whole corps of the rebels until Reynolds and a few of his staff rode up at a gallop and hailed Buford, who was with him in the steeple. The New York commission history (1900) and Bachelder (1873) tell the same scene without his name. No report of 1863 states it, and Weld's diary of 1863 has Reynolds talk with Buford in a field on the right of the road (T1-096): both are carried as scenarios. Jerome gives "seven A.M." and "half an hour" and no clock time for the meeting. Third reading of 2026-11-16: the National Park Service's HABS record of 1966 says that the Seminary cupola was used as a post of observation by Buford and Reynolds on Jul 1 (naming Wentz and Tilberg as its basis). Two later narratives give other orders of the scene and are carried as scenarios beside Jerome's: Wentz (1926: Buford alone in the cupola at the start, Reynolds there about an hour after the engagement began, then both ride out) and Doubleday (1882, printed by Hoke 1887: Buford in the steeple after an hour's fighting, Reynolds climbing up to him). No new source gives a clock time or the ladder. Still unsupported or open: A ladder led from the attic to the cupola in 1863 / Time of the meeting 09:30-10:20 / The ladder from the attic to the cupola; a clock time for the sighting and for Reynolds' arrival at the steeple (Jerome gives "seven A.M." and "half an hour"); Jerome's letter was read only as printed in a 1989 study, the original (Bachelder Papers, U.S. Army Military History Institute) was not seen.

title: T1-173: target 'the railroad cut' for Wiedrich's fire
desc: Row T1-173 (Jul 1 ≈17:00). Verdict corrected. Corrected claim: Wiedrich's battery stood on a hill north of the Baltimore turnpike near the cemetery and east of the town (Hunt: in front of the cemetery entrance). During the afternoon it skirmished with a rebel battery posted near the York road. About 5 p.m., when the Union infantry that had advanced through the town was repulsed, Wiedrich changed the direction of his pieces, opened with shells on the columns advancing from the town, and then fired canister at the enemy that appeared in front; the fire was kept up until late in the evening. Howard and Hunt place the enemy's single attempt to turn the right at about 4.30 p.m. and say Wiedrich's battery broke the line. Nothing in the reports ties this fire to the railroad cut (the cut lies on Oak Ridge, far from his front). Still unsupported or open: The target 'Confederates at the railroad cut' / Any target of Wiedrich's fire at 'the railroad cut' (not in any report); the source the seed cites is secondary and was not retrievable.
why: the seed target is not in any Official Records passage read; the reports give the hill north of the Baltimore pike and the columns advancing from the town. No non-lead source read supports the open part exactly (Law cl.4); not a physics limit.

title: T1-175: whether 'an hour since' in Hancock's 5.25 dispatch is a misprint
desc: Row T1-175 (Jul 1 17:25). Verdict corrected. title: T1-176: hour of Williams' turn toward the Hanover road and of his recall
desc: Row T1-176 (Jul 1 ≈17:30). Verdict corrected. Corrected claim: Slocum moved the corps to Two Taverns on the morning of Jul 1 and resumed the march when news came that the First and Eleventh Corps were engaged. Geary, at Two Taverns by 11 a.m., advanced at about 2 p.m., reported to Hancock, who sent him to the extreme left, and by 5 p.m. had two regiments of his First Brigade on the hills south and west of the town, the rest along the line to the Baltimore turnpike and the Second Brigade with two guns in reserve about 2 miles out; the division rested on its arms during the night. Williams' division was directed by a cross-road toward the Hanover road to take an eminence about a mile east of the town, found it held by the enemy and, when about to assault, was called back as the Union forces had retired behind the town; it bivouacked nearer the Baltimore pike. The seed's 'Geary takes position on Cemetery Ridge' and '17:30' do not match the reports (the left near Round Top; 14:00 advance, 17:00 in position). Still unsupported or open: Geary 'takes position on Cemetery Ridge' at about 17:30 / The hour at which Williams' division began to turn toward the Hanover road and the hour of the recall (no hour printed; only 'about sunset' for the later move) / Whether any XII Corps unit stood on Cemetery Ridge proper on Jul 1 (no report says so) / Geary's hour of advance is 2 p. m. on the page image of printed page 825; the OCR text of the archive.org item reads 3 p. m., which the first close-out and the seed's source chain carried (corrected here).

title: T1-186: Ewell's reasons 'narrow streets' and 'lack of support from Hill'
desc: Row T1-186 (Jul 1 evening). Verdict corrected. title: T1-188: date of establishment of Lee's headquarters at the Thompson house; building year; fence burning
desc: Row T1-188 (Jul 1 evening). Verdict partially_supported. Corrected claim: The National Park Service writes that the Mary Thompson House, built in the 1840s, served as Lee's headquarters and that on the morning of July 1, 1863 Lee rode just north of Gettysburg and established his headquarters in the farmstead residence of Mary Thompson. That differs from the seed's 'evening'; no Official Records passage names the Thompson house or gives Lee's place on the evening of Jul 1. The only place the sources name for Lee on the evening of Jul 1 is Early's account of a conference with Ewell and Rodes on the back porch of a small house north of the town near the Carlisle road. Longstreet (1896) reports to 'General Lee's head-quarters' at daylight on Jul 2 without naming a place. An illustration by Benson Lossing titled 'Confederate Headquarters' (a scene of September 1866, published in 1877) shows the repaired house (caption in the NPS landscape report); the same report says the house became famous for its association with Confederate headquarters following the Union retreat from Seminary Ridge on July 1, with the headquarters operations probably extending into the surrounding area, notably the Dustman orchard across the turnpike. The year of building (1833 Stone Sentinels; 1840s NPS), the 'Thaddeus Stevens building' reading of Wikipedia and the burning of Mary Thompson's fences for firewood have no passage in the local texts and stay unsupported. The seed calls Lee-in-the-cupola a rumour. Jacobs (1864, p.41) writes, in his account of Jul 3 before the 2.30 p.m. cannonade, that 'during the day General Lee had reconnoitred our position from the College cupola'; that is the statement of one resident, with no source given, for Jul 3 and not for the evening of Jul 1, and no cupola scene is shown for Jul 1. Added by the second reading: a relief worker's letter of the consecration day (Nov 1863) says the party 'saw Lee's headquarters' on Seminary Hill; Hoke (1887) places Lee's headquarters in a stone house a short distance out on the Chambersburg Pike and says Lee took observations from the cupola of Pennsylvania College (a later book; no day, no hour, no house named). Still unsupported or open: Mary Thompson's fences were burned for firewood (date not stated) / The house was built in 1833 (Stone Sentinels page named in the seed) / The date and hour of establishment at the Thompson house; the building's year beyond the NPS 1840s (the seed's 1833 is a lead); the fence burning; any report naming the Thompson house on Jul 1.
why: no Official Records passage and no library text before 1900 names the Thompson house on Jul 1; the NPS article says morning, the seed says evening. No non-lead source read supports the open part exactly (Law cl.4); not a physics limit.

title: T1-197: Jul 1 night share of the damage in Evergreen Cemetery; iron fences and monuments
desc: Row T1-197 (Jul 1 NIGHT). Verdict partially_supported. Corrected claim: The National Park Service landscape report says: troops began to arrive on Cemetery Hill on July 1 when Howard posted a reserve of his Eleventh Corps; late in the day, as Union troops retreated, they reinforced the defensive lines around Cemetery Hill; lines of artillery were positioned near the summit along the northern and western borders of Evergreen Cemetery with caissons and horses among the grave plots; it was reported that General Howard ordered troops to lay the headstones flat on the ground to prevent their destruction; troops tore down wood and stone fences and rebuilt stone fences as breastworks. Battle damage included bullet holes and cracks in some grave markers, damage to grave-plot fences, removal of planks from the fences along the Baltimore pike, and a damaged gatehouse. The report does not date the laying flat of the headstones or the fence damage within the three days, says nothing of 'iron fences', and names no monument destroyed. The seed's attribution of the night of Jul 1 is therefore not documented; the damage is shown as occurring during the battle, with the evening of Jul 1 as the earliest time. Added by the second reading: newspapers of July 1863 say that in the cannonade of Jul 3 the tombstones were knocked over and iron railings torn (Boston Journal's correspondent, printed Jul 23), that tombstones and beautiful monuments were demolished (Bellows Falls Times, Jul 10), and that monuments and headstones lay overturned and graves were trampled by horses (Chicago Daily Tribune, Jul 12); none dates this damage to the evening of Jul 1. The row's design hypotheses remain hypotheses. title: T1-217: hour of the relief of Buford's division on Jul 2 and Gamble's bivouac on the night of Jul 1
desc: Row T1-217 (Jul 1 NIGHT). Verdict corrected. Corrected claim: Buford: after placing his command on the extreme left he went to Cemetery Hill where Hancock arrived; 'my division bivouacked that night on the left of our position, with pickets extending almost to Fairfield'; on Jul 2 the division engaged the enemy's sharpshooters on the left and held its own until relieved by Sickles' corps, after which it moved to Taneytown and bivouacked for the night; on Jul 3 it moved to Westminster to guard the trains. Devin: ordered to the extreme left, where the brigade bivouacked for the night; on Jul 2 the Third Corps coming into position, the brigade was ordered to Taneytown. Pleasonton: Buford's division held a position on the left until relieved by the Third Corps, 'when it was directed to take post at Westminster'. Merritt's Reserve Brigade marched to Emmitsburg on the 2d. The seed's alternatives (Taneytown, Emmitsburg, Westminster) are different units and days: Taneytown the night of Jul 2 (Buford, Devin), Westminster Jul 3 and as the directed post (Pleasonton), Emmitsburg the Reserve Brigade (Merritt). The hour of the relief on Jul 2 is not printed; Birney's relief of Geary at 7 a.m. gives the earliest hour for the Third Corps' line (T1-194). Still unsupported or open: The hour of the relief on Jul 2 and Gamble's own bivouac on the night of Jul 1 / The hour of the relief of Buford's division on Jul 2; Gamble's bivouac on the night of Jul 1.
why: Buford and Devin give the left-flank bivouac and the Jul 2 relief without an hour; Gamble's report is silent. No non-lead source read supports the open part exactly (Law cl.4); not a physics limit.

title: T1-219: moon mostly hidden, darkest of the three nights, dew and fog in the low ground
desc: Row T1-219 (Jul 1-2 NIGHT). Verdict partially_supported. Corrected claim: Evening: Jacobs's record as relayed in 1885 (second-hand) has the sky covered with cirro-stratus at 9 p.m. and the thermometer at 74. Night: Everett says the full moon was veiled by thin clouds; Burling, at Emmitsburg, says the night was so very dark that his brigade could not march before about 4 a.m. after orders at 1.30 a.m.; the computed moon stood 30 degrees high from midnight to 2 a.m. (98.6-98.3 percent lit). title: T2-001: strength of O. Smith's brigade ('about 1,600 fresh') and Hancock's 'send every man'
desc: Row T2-001 (Jul 1 ~16:00). Verdict corrected. Corrected claim: Butterfield's order of 1.10 p.m.: Hancock to turn over the Second Corps to Gibbon, go to the front and, if Reynolds is dead, 'assume command of the corps there assembled, viz, the Eleventh, First, and Third, at Emmitsburg', advising Meade whether the ground is a better one to fight on. Hancock: at 3 p.m. he arrived at Gettysburg and assumed command; Wadsworth's division and a battery were placed on the eminence across the turnpike. Howard (dispatch): Hancock arrived at 4 p.m. Hunt (BL-3, 1888): Wadsworth led the 7th Indiana to Culp's Hill; Hancock, received at the hill, ordered Wadsworth at once to Culp's Hill to secure the position. Doubleday: Hancock directed him to send a force to support a battery on a lower range of hills some 100 yards east; he sent the rest of Wadsworth's division, then Howard's counter-orders caused delay. Smith: his brigade, formed in mass in rear of the hill, advanced through the cemetery to the front of the hill overlooking the town; its arrival 'in good order and with full ranks' contributed to holding the hill. The seed's 'about 1,600 fresh' and 'tells Doubleday to send every man' are not in these reports; the arrival hours 15:00, before 16:00, 16:00 and 16:30 are carried as scenarios under the recorded default C-039 (about 15:00-16:00). Still unsupported or open: O. Smith's brigade numbered about 1,600 fresh men; Hancock told Doubleday to send every man / 'about 1,600 fresh' for O. Smith's brigade; 'tells Doubleday to send every man'.

title: T2-003: hour of take-over, first wounded and counts other than 1,800 and 1,900 at the Spangler farm hospital
desc: Row T2-003 (Jul 1 mid-afternoon). Verdict partially_supported. Corrected claim: Documented: the Eleventh Corps hospital occupied the house and farm of Geo.
